newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African trade surplus back on track in March.
newsitem.headline: S.African trade surplus back on track in March.

text.p: South Africa's trade balance moved back into a healthy surplus in March after a deficit in February, restoring economists' confidence in a sharply reduced 1997 current account deficit.
South African Revenue Service figures released on Friday showed a trade surplus of 1.98 billion rand in March from a 451.6 million rand deficit in February.
On the export side there were healthy increases in machinery, transport equipment and chemical products, underlining a reported pick-up in overseas manufacturing sales this year.
Kevin Lings of Nedcor said there may have been delays in some of the February export figures which only came through last month, but on a three-month basis the position was encouraging.
"On a rolling three-month basis the picture looks quite good. It indicates an overall better trade performance and a much improved current account deficit," he said.
"I think we will see a continued improvement in exports this year, not among agricultural commodities or gold, but among manufactured goods."
The cumulative trade surplus for the first three months of the year stood at 2.045 billion rand or 682 million a month -- double the monthly average of 327 million in the comparable year-ago period.

The volatile precious stones and metals category of exports, which includes diamond sales from neighbouring Botswana, showed a three billion rand increase in March, to 8.947 billion rand on a cumulative basis, but this was in line with the previous two months.
The South African Revenue Service currently includes trade data from Botswana, Lesotho, Namibia and Swaziland in its South African figures.
Economists have complained this makes it difficult to guage the state of South Africa's current account balance.
Botswana's figures in particular, which mainly consist of diamond exports, often result in South African trade figures being highly volatile on a month-to-month basis.
But the department is developing programmes which would separate the data, a process which the department expects to take two to three months.
Economists surveyed by Reuters last month predicted South Africa would show a current account deficit of 3.65 billion rand in 1997, down from 8.5 billion in 1996.
